title: Midterm Elections Live Updates: Democrats Project Power as G.O.P. Reels in a Reordered Washington
byline: Jess Bidgood, Catie Edmondson, Kellen Browning, Amy Harmon, Heather Knight, Shawn Hubler, Bayliss Wagner, Chris Cameron, Emily Cochrane, Caroline Soler, Christine Zhang, Annie Karni, Scott Dance, Carl Hulse, Nina Agrawal, Lauren McGaughy, Mitch Smith, Patricia Mazzei, Soumya Karlamangla, Erica L. excerpt: Representative Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the next House speaker, said his party would focus on affordability after seizing control of Congress. President Trump focused on his renovation projects as Republicans grasped for answers.

Here’s the latest.

A new political era opened in Washington on Wednesday, as Democrats vowed to use their sweeping majority to check President Trump’s power, while prominent Republicans blamed their midterm wipeout on his agenda and party leadership.

Democrats were on track to secure at least a 50-seat majority in the House and solid control of the Senate after notching seismic victories around the country, in deep red House districts and long-Republican Senate seats. Vice President JD Vance blamed the rout on Mr. Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran, a remarkable break from a president who, for much of the past decade, has demanded total fealty from his party.

“Everyone knows why we lost,” Mr. Vance said on social media. For his part, Mr. Trump said Mr. Vance’s assessment was “largely true.” He added, “If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House, predicted Democrats would win at least 255 of the 435 seats in the chamber, comparing the scope of his party’s romp to an “American tsunami.” Democrats picked off Republicans who had not expected competitive races in conservative-leaning seats from Indiana to Missouri to Alabama, putting themselves on pace to make generational gains similar to those of the Republican wave of 1994 — only in reverse.

After two years of Republican control of Congress that reduced the House’s role to that of mere bystander, Mr. Jeffries promised to reassert the chamber’s power by undertaking aggressive investigations with oversight.

“The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” Mr. Jeffries promised.

Republicans lost Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Two other tight Senate contests haven’t been called: Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi, where roughly 1,100 votes separated the two candidates as of Wednesday evening.

The decisive control of the Senate is a “generational remake,” Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, told reporters in Washington.

Voters across every major demographic group — race, age, gender and education — made a drastic swing left in Tuesday’s election, reversing the gains Mr. Trump had made with them in 2024.

Mr. Trump seemed to brush off the sweeping repudiation. He used his first public appearance on Wednesday to tour the site of the ballroom he is building on the White House grounds. There, he defended what he considered to be his legacy-defining projects. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world,” he said.

The shock waves from the election reverberated more resoundingly among other Republicans, who had feared widespread losses but had not anticipated such a renunciation of their party.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana told aides that he would not seek to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, setting off a scramble among ambitious Republicans to succeed him. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio announced he would seek the role, arguing that Republicans needed to take a combative approach toward the Democratic majority next year.

“In these next two years, our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democrat party is,” he said. “Offense, not defense, wins elections.”

Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana also jumped into the contest, arguing that Republicans must act with more unity.

Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida said his fellow Republicans in Washington should have voted to release the Epstein files earlier and banned congressional stock trading. He called the election as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years.”

Mr. Trump told The New York Times in an interview late Tuesday night that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the midterm results and was prepared to work with Democrats — despite his repeated efforts to sow doubts about voter fraud and to have the Justice Department intervene in elections.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

  • Democratic landslide: The Democrats’ landslide did not just reach the federal races but also state and local governments. The party notched firsts in governors’ races and won down-ballot races like those for state treasurer, secretary of state and state legislature. Democrats are set to be in the majority in a dozen statehouse chambers where they had been the minority party.

  • G.O.P. bright spots: Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida, with Senator Ashley Moody defeating Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat. Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump supporter, was elected Florida’s first Black governor, keeping the Republicans’ hold on that office.

  • Ballot measures: Voters across the country also weighed in on a range of statewide issues, including abortion, how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted. Read more ›

Teresa Benitez-Thompson, a Democrat and former state legislator, defeated David Flippo, an Air Force veteran and financial adviser, according to The Associated Press, to win the open seat in Nevada’s open Second Congressional District, a conservative region in the northern part of the state.

The district has never been represented by a Democrat, but Flippo was plagued by a series of scandals related to his finances and accusations of stolen military valor, with even the district’s retiring Republican incumbent, Representative Mark Amodei, saying he would not vote for him.

Washington State voters have approved a ballot measure restricting transgender girls from participating in girls’ sports, The Associated Press reported. The measure has been widely viewed as a test of efforts to enact similar bans beyond the 27 Republican-led states where they are already in place.

In the race to replace Representative Nancy Pelosi in California’s 11th Congressional District, Connie Chan, a San Francisco supervisor, conceded to State Senator Scott Wiener on Wednesday after she fell further behind in the latest vote count. Both Wiener and Chan are liberal Democrats, but they split on housing and transit policy. Chan thanked Pelosi for her support and congratulated Wiener. The Associated Press has not yet called the race.

Nithya Raman widened her lead slightly over Mayor Karen Bass on Wednesday, as California’s notoriously slow vote count continued in the Los Angeles mayor’s race. Raman, a democratic socialist and former Bass ally on the City Council, was ahead 52-48 percent with a little more than two-thirds of the expected vote in.

These Republicans bet big on Trump. It didn’t pay off.

President Trump used to gloat about his near-perfect endorsement record, reveling in the control he exerted over the Republican nomination process during this year’s primary season. Voters overwhelmingly rewarded the candidates he backed and punished those who displeased him, muscling numerous less loyal candidates out of contention.

“If you pushed back” on Mr. Trump, said Justin Evans, a Republican strategist in South Carolina, “you’d get your head chopped off.”

Mr. Trump has little to brag about this week. Senate candidates he had helped elevate, including Darline Graham in South Carolina, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Ken Paxton in Texas, lost by margins previously unimagined by even the most optimistic Democrats. Those high-profile defeats contributed to what Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, a one-time Trump rival for the presidential nomination, called as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” as the country has seen in a century.

“The people who did the best last night were the people who distanced themselves from the president,” Mr. Evans said, calling the results “a universal repudiation of the bullying that’s been taking place during this primary” by Mr. Trump.

Here’s a look at what happened to some of the candidates who tied their fortunes most closely to Mr. Trump.

Darline Graham

After Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican, died in July, Mr. Trump threw his weight behind Mr. Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, in a snap primary election. While many Republican insiders objected, primary voters listened, narrowly nominating Ms. Graham over Representative Ralph Norman, despite her self-described lack of experience or policy expertise.

On Tuesday, the wider South Carolina electorate rejected Ms. Graham, choosing to send a Democrat to Washington for the first time in nearly 30 years.

“It wasn’t that voters rebuked Trump,” Mr. Evans said, noting that the Republican nominee for governor had earned at least 90,000 more votes than Ms. Graham. “It was that the entire Washington machine pushed this woman on South Carolina, and South Carolina resoundingly pushed back.”

Ken Paxton

Senate Republicans begged Mr. Trump to endorse Senator John Cornyn over Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, in the state’s Republican Senate primary. Many argued that Mr. Paxton’s scandal-ridden past would make it significantly more difficult, and more costly, to win in a general election. They also said a contentious intraparty battle would waste resources needed in more competitive states. Mr. Trump ignored them, waiting until days before a May primary runoff to back Mr. Paxton.

On Tuesday, despite dramatically outspending Democrats, Republicans lost the Senate seat, the governor’s mansion, and every other statewide race in Texas, breaking a more than three-decade-long streak of G.O.P. dominance.

Some Texas Republicans speculated that Mr. Paxton would have won the primary regardless of Mr. Trump’s choice. It is also not clear that Mr. Cornyn could have defied the tsunami of voter anger that propelled Democrats to victory up and down the ballot. But some blamed Mr. Paxton, and Mr. Trump, for the extent of the losses.

“You stand by Trump at your own peril at this point,” said Dade Phelan, the former Republican speaker of the State House. He recalled how Mr. Trump asked voters in Texas and elsewhere to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

“Well, voters imagined he was on the ballot,” Mr. Phelan said. “And it was an absolute apocalypse for Republicans.”

Michael Whatley

Mr. Trump’s fingerprints were all over North Carolina’s Senate race. First, Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who has served in North Carolina for more than a decade, announced he would retire rather than run for re-election after the president threatened to back a primary opponent against him.

Then, Mr. Trump handpicked Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, and Mr. Whatley spent millions touting Mr. Trump’s endorsement ahead of his victory in the Republican Senate primary. On Tuesday night, Mr. Whatley fell to former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, by around 20 points, a stunning leftward shift for a state that Mr. Trump won in 2024.

Meghan McMichael, 33, a voter in Canton, N.C., said on Tuesday that she had voted for Mr. Cooper and other Democrats in order to hold the Trump administration accountable for its treatment of immigrants, and the state of the economy.

“I’m just hopeful that certain people will be held accountable for things that have happened over the last two years,” she said.

Jon Husted

Senator Jon Husted, Ohio’s Republican Senate nominee and a former professional football player, was little known nationally until President Trump started talking about his rear end while on the campaign trail. Mr. Husted also joined Mr. Trump at several Ohio rallies in the final weeks of the campaign, tying himself to the president.

Mr. Husted lost to former Senator Sherrod Brown on Tuesday, making Ohio one of seven states that Democrats had flipped as of Wednesday evening.

The president’s comments about Mr. Husted’s backside may also have backfired, with voters across the country telling The New York Times they had disapproved of his remarks that Mr. Husted had a “great ass” and a “pile of muscle.”

In Lincoln, Neb., on Tuesday, Deondre Webster, 36, said he didn’t believe Mr. Trump is a good role model for his three daughters.

“We don’t want to see the leader of the country talking about male behinds or stuff like that onstage,” he said. “When he’s supposed to be the leader, and that’s not what we’re teaching our kids.”

Mark Barrett in North Carolina and Justin Diep in Nebraska contributed reporting.

“It’s so dark outside,” President Trump just wrote on social media. He wasn’t talking about the midterms, but a failed legislative effort to make daylight saving time permanent, which would have ended the semiannual time change that shortens winter days.

Continuing his effort to shrug off an overwhelming Republican defeat in Tuesday’s elections, Trump complained that the Senate had not passed the measure by Election Day, and that the clock change back to standard time had moved the sunset in Washington today to 5:06 p.m.

“Just a few days ago it was so nice and sunny at this same time,” Trump said in a post at 6:33 p.m., adding that “I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this prior to the Election because I didn’t want to have certain Senators lose their Race, in a landslide, but it is too bad they can’t get it done.”

He conceded that the country has “far bigger priorities” than making daylight saving time permanent, but added, “I will keep fighting for this!”

Many Republicans tied their fates to President Trump, only to suffer a rude awakening on Tuesday night. That included Mayes Middleton, the Republican nominee for Texas attorney general, who spent millions from his personal fortune to brand himself as “MAGA Mayes” during a Republican primary he ultimately won over Representative Chip Roy, an established Republican and former assistant attorney general, whom he branded as anti-Trump.

But Middleton lost soundly to a Democrat, Nathan Johnson, on Tuesday despite outspending him by more than six to one. In an interview, Johnson said he was “delighted when Mayes Middleton nicknamed himself ‘MAGA Mayes,’ because I saw this coming.”

Mississippi’s secretary of state, Michael Watson, has mapped out the wait ahead for votes to be counted in the tight contest between Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and Scott Colom, her Democratic challenger, who leads by 1,138 votes. There’s about 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots that have to be received within five business days, plus an “unknown number of affidavit ballots.” Counties have until Nov. 13 to submit certified results to the state.

What we know, and don’t, in the Alaska and Mississippi Senate vote counts.

Control of the U.S. Senate has already been determined, with 33 of the 35 contests being called within hours of polls closing. In Alaska and Mississippi, however, no race calls have been made for the Senate and it could be quite some time until either contest is decided, even as some additional vote totals trickle out in the coming days.

In both cases, the Democratic nominee is clinging to a slim lead, but the reasons for the lack of a call are far different.

What We Know in the Alaska Senate Race

Alaska’s Senate race could take days or weeks to be called. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, had a lead of fewer than 1,000 votes as of Wednesday afternoon, but nearly a quarter of the expected votes remain uncounted.

The bulk of the remaining vote is in the form of mail-in ballots. Some were cast close to Election Day, while others were postmarked by Election Day and will be received in the days after. A smaller chunk of early in-person ballots are also outstanding.

The deadline to tabulate all ballots, including provisional ballots, is Nov. 18. That is also the date that ranked-choice tabulation will begin, should neither Ms. Peltola nor Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, cross the 50 percent threshold needed to win the election in the first round.

While the late mail vote typically leans toward Democrats, multiple factors could undercut Ms. Peltola’s possible advantage, including how many ballots will be received and how many are from voters who did not rank additional candidates beyond their first choice. There is also the potentially confounding presence of the other two candidates on the ballot, Gerald L. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

A New York Times analysis of the available ranked-choice data pulled from each voter’s ballot shows that more than a third of voters who ranked Mr. Heikes or Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. as their first choice did not rank another candidate. That means these ballots would not count toward either Ms. Peltola or Senator Sullivan in subsequent rounds of the ranked-choice tabulation.

What We Know in the Mississippi Senate Race

As of Wednesday evening, Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee in Mississippi, had a lead of roughly 1,000 votes over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent. Because the margin is so tight, The Associated Press may not be able to make a race call until the state certifies a winner.

Mississippi is somewhat of an outlier in that it does not have a mechanism for automatic recounts, and has no method for a candidate to contest the election, so a court order would be required to initiate a recount.

Nearly all of the votes have been counted in the race, but a smattering of provisional ballots — which are ballots given to those with questions about their eligibility to vote — are still waiting to be counted, as are some late-arriving mail ballots. According to Mississippi's secretary of state, there are approximately 3,600 outstanding mail ballots that could arrive in time to be counted.

Mississippi’s Supreme Court ruled in June that the state must accept mail-in ballots that arrive by the Tuesday after Election Day — this year, Nov. 10. And provisional ballots in the state must be tallied by that day as well. For a provisional ballot to be accepted, the voter is required to provide proper identification to elections officials, obtain a state voter ID card, or submit a religious exemption.

Some counties in the state have said they hope to begin releasing some results of provisional ballots on Wednesday. It is currently unknown how many ballots remain uncounted statewide. Adding a layer of complexity, ballot processing and counting, which includes ruling on provisional ballots, is conducted by each county’s five-person elections commission rather than a single elections official.

In 2024, the state had just under 15,000 provisional ballots, of which 70 percent were accepted. In 2022, the state had about 5,700 provisional ballots, of which 75 percent were accepted.

Evan Peng contributed reporting.

A G.O.P. group says the party faces a ‘crisis-level’ loss of elected women.

A group that champions electing conservative women to public office issued a blunt warning to Republicans on Wednesday after the Democratic sweep of Congress, calling the defeats of a large number of G.O.P. women an emergency that must be addressed.

“We are once again facing a crisis-level decline in Republican women in Congress,” Danielle Barrow, the president of Winning For Women Action Fund, an outside group dedicated to electing Republican women, said in a statement.

Ms. Barrow sounded the alarm as Democrats were celebrating their own milestone of electing more than 100 women to the House for the first time in history.

Republicans already have far less gender diversity in their ranks in the House, where there are currently 32 G.O.P. women (including two nonvoting delegates) — around 15 percent of their members.

With the landslide Democratic victories that are projected to win them the largest House majority in decades, that number could potentially dip to below 20 next year, after all races are called.

In 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected just one new G.O.P. woman to Congress, the party made a commitment to recruit and invest in female candidates, Ms. Barrow said. It worked: Two years later, 11 of the 15 seats Republicans flipped were by women.

“But that commitment to recruiting women faded when the urgency did,” she said. “Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve. It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

Democrats eye inquiries into Trump actions on energy, public land.

Democrats in Congress are poised to ramp up investigations into Trump administration efforts to limit renewable energy development, promote fossil fuels and mining, and open up public lands to commercial interests.

Before the elections, House Democrats had already announced probes into some of those actions, including a $1 billion payout to cancel offshore wind farms, cuts to renewable energy investments in Puerto Rico and the shrinking of two national monuments in Utah. In other cases, they have raised allegations of corruption against officials overseeing public lands, fisheries and offshore energy development.

But with a majority in Congress next year, they can deepen those inquiries, said Representative Jared Huffman, Democrat of California, who stands to be chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee as its current ranking member. In January, Democrats will gain power to convene hearings, call witnesses to testify under oath and go to court to compel cooperation by the executive branch. Under Republican control, Congress has not used those powers to look into the Trump administration.

Just in the hours since the scope of the Democratic gains became clear, outside groups also began clamoring for new inquiries into steps by the administration to limit enforcement of pollution regulations and reduce the flow of federal disaster aid.

Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, said such investigations could help deliver on his party’s campaign promises to promote affordability. The Trump administration’s efforts to purge the government of any focus on climate change have contributed to rising property insurance premiums and energy costs, Mr. Whitehouse said.

“Democrats will work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors through their climate denial fraud and corrupting dark money influence,” Mr. Whitehouse said in a statement.

The Environmental Protection Network, a nonpartisan group of hundreds of former Environmental Protection Agency officials, called for investigations into Trump administration pollution-limit rollbacks and rule exemptions. The group said the administration has ignored scientific evidence and its own experts to put industry above public health.

Samantha Montano, a professor of emergency management at the Massachusetts Maritime Academy who has criticized the Trump administration’s disaster management policy, said Democrats should investigate staffing cuts at the Federal Emergency Management Agency, as well as the agency’s distribution of key preparedness grants and recovery funding. Analyses have shown a partisan bias in President Trump’s approval of federal disaster declarations, which unlock FEMA aid for communities.

‘I was caught up in the Trump tsunami’: Susan Collins speaks about losing her Senate seat.

As Susan Collins campaigned in York County, Maine, recently, a woman approached to inform the Republican senator that she had always supported her and “absolutely” loved her. But she wasn’t going to vote for her this time.

“She said it was the only way she could send a message to Trump,” Ms. Collins recounted in an interview on Wednesday, a day after she lost to the Democrat Troy Jackson in her attempt to win a sixth term.

That was the story of the election for Ms. Collins, the chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee and a force in the Senate for three decades.

“I was caught up in the Trump tsunami that swept away many incumbent Republican senators who have served their states well for many years and really care about our country,” she said.

The five-term Republican senator had long seemed invulnerable to the ordinary laws of politics because of her singular political brand as a New England centrist with a gift for constituent service and an ability to steer federal dollars back home. In 2008, she triumphed in Maine while Barack Obama was romping and other Republicans were falling. In 2020, it seemed like her number might be up when polls had her down against a well-funded state lawmaker, but she again won easily.

Democrats saluted ruefully in respect.

But 2026 turned out to be a different case entirely as Ms. Collins was brought down by a combination of factors, most of which were attributable to President Trump and the war with Iran. There were soaring fuel prices in a state reliant on home heating oil. The punishing tariffs the president imposed on neighboring Canada. An immigration crackdown that resulted in a fatal shooting by federal agents in one Maine community. And always the perception that she wasn’t doing enough to stand up to the president, even when she was one of the few Republicans to occasionally break with him.

“Everybody ignores the fact that I voted to convict him in the second impeachment trial,” Ms. Collins said. “What bigger break could there be? It is never enough. I want results and they want angry rhetoric.”

On top of dissatisfaction that she hadn’t distanced herself sufficiently from the president, some voters harbored resentment about her vote in 2018 to confirm Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, given his later role in overturning Roe v. Wade.

The coming result was evident from talking to voters on Tuesday as they exited the central polling place in Bangor — home turf for Ms. Collins. Several of them said they had repeatedly marked their ballots for “our senator,” as her ubiquitous yard signs proclaimed, but they would not do so this time.

“This time,” said Deborah Hanson of Bangor, “I’ve got to try something new. Susan Collins has voted with Trump on so many things.”

“To me, it is a close thing,” said Bob Kelly, another longtime Bangor voter. “But I can’t support anybody that supports Trump.”

In rejecting Ms. Collins, Maine voters gave up a tremendous amount of influence over federal spending by turning out the woman at the helm of the influential committee that controls federal spending. It is unusual but not unheard-of for voters to reject senior leaders.

Voters in Washington State dumped Representative Tom Foley, a Democrat, when he was speaker of the House in 1994. Senator Tom Daschle, the Democratic leader, lost his re-election bid to Senator John Thune, now the majority leader, in South Dakota in 2004.

Ms. Collins leaned heavily on her role in spending as she campaigned around the state, visiting the fire stations, community projects and infrastructure improvements for which she had secured funding, noting that if she were no longer in office, that money might dry up.

“I wanted to make sure people know what their choice was,” she said.

The man who defeated her, Mr. Jackson, will be a junior member of the Senate with little ability to steer to the state anywhere near the kind of financial aid that Ms. Collins had helped win.

“What she has been able to do over the last six years is extraordinary,” said Steve Abbott, her campaign manager and longtime senior aide. “Every town you go to, you see a project that was funded and work that needed to be done. That’s an opportunity that the state has walked away from.”

Up until the end, Ms. Collins and her team had hoped they could pull out a win as they watched from a hotel suite in Bangor. They had been cheered by the “rock star” reception they received around the state, an outpouring they said was better than during some of her winning races in the past.

“We went all over the state and I’ve got to tell you, the crowds were huge, the reception was warm and the response could not have been better,” Ms. Collins said as she addressed and thanked supporters in Bangor before the results were known.

But results from the Democratic stronghold of Portland overwhelmed her.

The race was chaotic, and Ms. Collins and her advisers like to note that they basically had to run against three opponents: Gov. Janet Mills, who initially appeared to be the likely challenger before she dropped out; the oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary but dropped out after sexual abuse allegations; and Mr. Jackson, who had lost the state’s Democratic primary for governor but was then selected to replace Mr. Platner on the ballot.

Democrats have been frustrated for years both by Ms. Collins herself and their inability to defeat her. They poured huge amounts of money into the campaign, trying to highlight her ties to Mr. Trump and her votes for his policies. Ms. Collins pushed back, noting her own differences with the president on the Iran war, tariffs, the immigration crackdown and safety net cuts.

Over the course of her career, Ms. Collins was at the center of many major legislative negotiations on such tough issues as gun safety, health care and, following the Jan. 6, 2021, assault at the Capitol, a bill overhauling how electoral votes were counted. Her absence in the Senate will be felt on big legislative fights. She has not missed a vote in her Senate tenure.

Her political career was inspired in part by Margaret Chase Smith, the Maine Republican who served in the Senate from 1949 to 1972. Ms. Collins once met Ms. Smith, who had delivered a famous denunciation of Joseph McCarthy, and noted that some constituents encouraged her to have a Smith-like moment of conscience when it came to Mr. Trump.

“I would argue that I have, like Margaret Chase Smith, taken a lot of tough votes and stood up for what I believe in,” she said. “But I think the best comparison is we each lost our last race for the Senate.

“I have now had my Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

Among the Democratic winners in Tuesday night’s elections: More medical professionals.

About a half-dozen Democrats who flipped Republican congressional seats are doctors and nurses, many of whom made health policy and their opposition to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s agenda central to their campaigns.

Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, a pediatrician, repeatedly called out Mr. Kennedy as her “archnemesis.” She and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan appear to be the first Democrats with medical degrees elected to the Senate in about 60 years.

In California, Representative-elect Richard Pan, a pediatrician and a former state legislator who worked to tighten vaccine exemptions, beat the incumbent, Kevin Kiley, a former Republican who this year ran as an independent.

“This election cycle, R.F.K. Jr. was hands down our No. 1 recruitment and fund-raising tool,” said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action, an organization that spent $30 million to support Democratic scientists and health care professionals.

Other successful health care candidates who flipped House districts include Kristina Knickerbocker, an oncology nurse practitioner in Ohio, and Mitchell Berman, a former Veterans Affairs nurse in Wisconsin. Amish Shah, an emergency room physician, appears to be on track to win in a competitive Arizona district, and Adam Hamawy, a plastic surgeon, won a safe Democratic seat in New Jersey.

Their success reflects, in part, the overall momentum of Democrats in Tuesday’s election. “It was a good thing to be a Democrat last night,” said Kristoffer Shields, director of the Eagleton Science and Politics Program at Rutgers-New Brunswick. Still, they ran, at least in part, on their credibility as medical professionals, “and it clearly seems to have worked,” he said.

They will join several Democratic medical professionals who have been elected since 2018, when a smaller wave of doctors and scientists ran in opposition to President Trump’s first administration.

“You could see a doctors’ caucus here in the Democratic Party,” Dr. Shields said. Just as the candidates were credible on health care to voters, “they’re going to be credible to other senators, or other representatives, once they get into Congress,” he said. He expects that among their top priorities will be making health care through the Affordable Care Act more affordable, perhaps by reinstating the subsidies that expired last year, and streamlining insurance processes to benefit patients.

I talked exclusively to Senator Susan Collins in the wake of her defeat, and she said she had been swept away in the anti-Trump wave. The Maine Republican has long defied political gravity, but voters in the state who had backed her repeatedly said they couldn’t do it this time — not because of Collins, but because of Trump.

She also compared herself to Margaret Chase Smith, the Maine senator who inspired her career and is known for having delivered a sharp denunciation of Joseph McCarthy. Collins said that she, too, had “taken a lot of tough votes and stood up for what I believe in.” But the best comparison, she noted, was that they both ultimately lost their last Senate race.

Texas Democrats prepare to relearn a skill: how to govern.

For Texas Democrats, the hits just keep on coming.

After routing Republicans in every statewide race and overturning a generation of conservative, one-party rule, the Democrats have also taken control of the Texas House of Representatives. The last time they held the majority in either legislative chamber was 2003.

Republicans will keep their majority in the Texas Senate. But the lieutenant governor, who, as the president of that chamber, is arguably the single most powerful force in lawmaking, will also be a Democrat: Vikki Goodwin. So is the governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa.

For the first time in about 25 years, Texas Democrats will have a real chance to govern. “Democrats have to deliver,” Gene Wu, the chairman of the Texas House Democratic Caucus, said from his home in Houston on Wednesday morning. “No excuses, no whining, no crying.”

Mr. Wu was wasting no time. He planned to drive to the state capital, Austin, on Wednesday to prepare for the next legislative session in January.

The Texas Legislature meets only once every two years, making the pressure especially high on Democrats to deliver real policymaking wins — and quickly. They’ve promised to focus their attention on pocketbook issues like taxes and education funding.

For a dozen years, Republicans forced Texas further to the right. Conservative legislators outlawed abortion, banned diversity offices in colleges, legalized the open carrying of firearms on their campuses, and stripped rights from the state’s gay community. They targeted big cities, all run by Democrats, by restricting local control.

Gov. Greg Abbott and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick led those efforts. Both men lost their re-election bids.

Mr. Wu said his party’s wins were a rebuke to big government policies that he said have come to define the modern Republican Party.

“We’re going to let cities decide if they want to have rainbow sidewalks again,” Mr. Wu said, referencing recent Republican-enforced bans on such displays.

Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat first elected before women could easily have credit cards, is the early favorite for House speaker. She would be the first Black Texan and the first woman in the role.

Tom Oliverson, the chairman of the House Republican Caucus, said the future for his party looked brighter than the present.

“When you kind of hit the bottom,” he said, “you can only go up from there, right?”

Democrats have flipped a second statewide office in Indiana. The A.P. called the state comptroller race for Jessica Bailey, who defeated the Republican incumbent, Elise Nieshalla. The comptroller had been referred to as the state auditor until a recent law change.

Indiana Democrats had been shut out of statewide office for years, but in the midterm elections have now won both the comptroller race and the secretary of state’s office. The party also flipped a Republican-held congressional seat in the Indianapolis suburbs and ousted several Republican state legislators, including the speaker of the House, who tried and failed last year to enact a new U.S. House map at President Trump’s request.

Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Republican, leads Eliott Rodriguez, her Democratic challenger, by 0.46 percentage points, which, if it holds, could meet Florida’s threshold for an automatic machine recount, which is half a percentage point.

On Wednesday, the elections supervisor in the county said her office was still dealing with 202 mail ballots in the race with signature discrepancies, which voters have until Thursday afternoon to cure. The elections office is also reviewing provisional ballots, her office said. The local canvassing board will handle those matters in a meeting on Friday. If needed, the Florida secretary of state could order a recount by Saturday.

Representative Jimmy Gomez, a California Democrat who has been in Congress for almost a decade and was accused of sexual misconduct this summer, has lost his House seat representing part of Los Angeles, according to The Associated Press. He was defeated by Angela Gonzales-Torres, an anti-establishment candidate from his own party endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America.

A day after a stinging midterm defeat, Trump focuses on his ballroom.

As his party reeled from a resounding defeat in the midterm elections, President Trump made an impromptu appearance on Wednesday at the White House, where he defended two of what he considers to be legacy-defining projects: his ballroom and the war in Iran.

Mr. Trump’s appearance at the ballroom’s construction site — his first comments to reporters since the American electorate delivered a sharp rebuke of his party and policies — was a ceremony to celebrate the raising of the final steel beam atop the structure. He delivered extensive remarks detailing the progress of the project before adding his signature to the beam. He never mentioned the results of the midterms.

“This is a special structure,” he said. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world.”

The beam-signing ceremony was the latest in a series of striking examples of the disconnect between Mr. Trump’s priorities and those of the American electorate. On Monday, the eve of the election, Mr. Trump gave a speech from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he spent nearly an hour detailing renovations he had ordered at sites around Washington rather than offer a closing argument to voters concerned by his handling of the economy and the war with Iran.

“You know, it was sort of mentioned a little bit during the campaign: ‘Why does Trump spend time on the White House?’” he said of his extensive renovations. “Well, first of all, it’s very little time. Second of all, I like it. It’s good. For me, it’s relaxing.”

After adding his signature to the giant steel beam and watching workers lift it into place on Wednesday, Mr. Trump addressed questions from reporters about the election results. He said that Vice President JD Vance’s assessment that Republicans had lost the election because of the war in Iran was “largely true” because the conflict had driven up gas prices, but said that he would make the same decision again.

“The Iran thing, we had to do,” he said, “and we continue to do it.”

Mr. Trump said that he looked forward to working with the Democratic-controlled Congress that was just elected, unless the Democrats sought to be “destructive,” in which case he would exercise his veto powers.

Asked if he was worried at all about a possible impeachment, Mr. Trump said, “No, not even a little bit.”

Later in the day, the president took to social media to complain that the Senate had not passed a legislative effort to make daylight saving time permanent, which would have ended the semiannual time change that shortens winter days, and that the clock change back to standard time had moved the sunset in Washington, D.C., today to 5:06 p.m.

“It’s so dark outside,” President Trump wrote.

The Democratic wave swept statehouses across the country.

The Democratic surge on Tuesday netted at least 330 state legislative seats, from New Hampshire to Arizona, giving the Democrats full control of 22 state governments and making them the majority in a dozen statehouse chambers where they had been the minority party.

And while Washington remains divided, Democrats will have the power to make policy on health care, voting and taxation in state capitals that for years have been far beyond their control, such as Texas, Georgia and North Carolina.

In Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Nevada, Democrats will hold both statehouse chambers as well as the governorship. The party was on the verge of the same “trifecta” in Arizona as well.

“Our victories have shattered Republicans’ grip on our statehouses,” said Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee.

The victories in state legislative races rarely grab national headlines, but statehouses exert enormous influence on issues that directly affect day-to-day life, from health care coverage to transportation. Some of those wins were the fruits of long rebuilding efforts. In Wisconsin, the fight to dismantle a Republican gerrymander of legislative districts finally delivered the Democrats both the State Senate and House, while the party retained the governor's office.

Elsewhere, state-level victories were almost incidental consequences of a wave that was bigger than even the most optimistic Democrat has anticipated.

The Arizona Senate’s minority leader, Priya Sundareshan, went to sleep Tuesday night with a statement saying she looks forward to seeing the votes counted. By morning, it was clear the changes would be huge.

“I’m really excited to be in the driver’s seat,” Ms. Sundareshan said.

Even in several states where Democrats did not win a majority, they still won enough seats to prevent Republican supermajorities, which confer the ability to override a governor’s veto.

Most notable were Iowa, where Rob Sand, a Democrat, won the governor’s race, and Ohio, where, Amy Acton, also a Democrat, was elected governor. They are their states’ first Democratic governors in 16 years, and with no Republican supermajority, both will have more leverage than they would otherwise have had.

State legislators allocate billions of dollars for schools, prisons and health care, and can shape policies on everything from data centers to taxes before Congress does. In Wisconsin, one of 10 states that have not expanded Medicaid access under the Affordable Care Act, Democrats now have the power to do so. But even in Texas and Georgia, the new Democratic governor and the one Democratic chamber will almost certainly apply enormous pressure to expand Medicaid as citizens struggle with health care costs.

And while legislative elections are typically overshadowed by midterm races for governor and Congress, this year’s races did command more attention — and money, including $100 million from the States Project, a Democratic group — in part because of the frenzied mid-decade U.S. House redistricting. Now the question of redistricting moves to the 2028 election, and the prospect of redrawing even more congressional maps, this time by Democrats.

The weakening of the Voting Rights Act by the Supreme Court in April had raised the prospects of states such as Texas and Georgia taking up redistricting again with an eye on diluting Democratic districts drawn to give Black and Hispanic voters more power. Now that those states have divided governments, a Republican redistricting would be impossible.

But Wisconsin and Pennsylvania could turn the tables on Republicans if their Democratic leaders choose to.

The earliest tally of state legislative results has Democrats netting at least 330 statehouse seats, but the number is sure to climb, perhaps as high as 800 seats. There is little doubt they will outperform 2018, when they gained more than 300 during Mr. Trump’s first term.

It was likely the best Democratic result since they gained more than 600 seats in 1974, right after Watergate, said Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting for the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Republicans gingerly pointed to President Trump’s abysmal approval ratings and the same headwinds of inflation, war and fuel costs that cost them the U.S. House and Senate, but also to governor’s races that went badly for the G.O.P.

“The national political environment and the impact of top-of-the-ticket races significantly affected our candidates’ ability to defy historical trends,” Edith Jorge-Tuñón, president of the Republican State Leadership Committee, said in a statement.

It remains to be seen whether the final tally will be as seismic as 2010, when Republicans unleashed their Redistricting Majority Project, or Redmap, and flipped 22 chambers and more than 700 seats — a “shellacking,” as former President Barack Obama described it.

That pendulum swing enabled Republicans to redraw maps and over the next decade to enact conservative policies to weaken labor unions, cut taxes, restrict voter access and expand education vouchers.

The president’s party has lost statehouse seats in 20 of the last 22 midterms, so Tuesday’s results were hardly a surprise, though a year ago the Republican State Leadership Committee held out hope for gains in Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania. Insead, all three of those statehouses will be completely in Democratic hands all with Democratic governors.

Democrats have done well in special elections to fill state legislative seats, but Democratic voters historically have chosen candidates at the top of the ticket, while leaving down- ballot races blank. That was not the case, however, on Tuesday.

And on a night full of unexpected results, one standout was North Carolina. Only three years ago, Democratic legislators were in a superminority, after State Representative Tricia Cotham, a Democrat, switched parties and gave Republicans the power to override former Gov. Roy Cooper’s veto and enact the state’s most restrictive abortion policy in 50 years.

After the Democrats broke that North Carolina supermajority in 2024, their goal for this year’s midterms was simply to chip away at the Republican majority in one of the country’s most gerrymandered states.

Instead, bolstered by Mr. Cooper’s resounding victory for U.S. Senate, they seized control of the House and narrowed the gap in the Senate, bolstering Mr. Cooper’s Democratic successor, Gov. Josh Stein. Ms. Cotham lost her seat.

A similar dynamic unfolded in Georgia and Texas, where Democrats won both states’ Houses of the Representatives for the first time since the early 2000s, as part of a sweep of all statewide races, as well as the governorships

History was also on the verge of being made in Arizona, as Democrats appeared poised to claim both the House and Senate, as one of six new trifectas. Arizona Democrats have not had an outright majority in any chamber since the early 1990s, and not had full control since the mid-1960s.

And though Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont, a popular moderate Republican, won a record sixth term, statehouse Democrats regained the supermajority they had lost in 2024.

Victories by Mr. Scott and Gov. Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were among the few bright spots for Republicans. They also held firm in conservative strongholds like Wyoming, Montana, Idaho and the Dakotas.

Still, there were cracks in Republican redoubts. In Missouri, Democrats broke the supermajority in both the House and Senate. And in Arkansas, Democrats gained a projected 10 seats in the State House.

Last week, Jay Morgan, a former chairman of the Georgia Republican Party, said the national outlook looked dire.

“There’s the potential of a total washout,” he said. “There are seats in play that nobody thought would be in play.”

He was proved right.

Sejal Govindarao contributed reporting.

Voters across every major demographic group — race, age, gender and education — made a drastic swing left in Tuesday’s election, reversing the broad shift in support that Republicans saw in 2024.

The reversal was most notable among young voters and voters of color, particularly Hispanic voters, who swung toward the Democratic Party by nearly 30 percentage points. Democrats also made sizable gains among groups typically seen as stalwarts of the Republican base — white voters without a college degree and older voters — both of which swung left.

The Senate race is extremely close in Mississippi, but the state has no vote recount law.

An unusual situation could be brewing in Mississippi, the only state in the country with no legal provision that allows for a recount of votes in a statewide election.

The Democratic candidate for Senate, Scott Colom, had a narrow 65-vote lead over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, in the afternoon. His lead grew to 1,138 by the evening, but Mississippi’s secretary of state reported that about 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots could still arrive within the allotted five business days, and that there were also an “unknown number of affidavit ballots.”

Some 47 states have a provision for an automatic recount if a contest is close or if a candidate requests a recount. Two more states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.

Most state recount provisions were instituted during the last century as a result of legal challenges that made their way to state supreme courts. But Mississippi has no recount law on the books, leaving it unprepared to handle a particularly close election.

There are still small batches of ballots to be counted in the state, and the margin between the candidates may widen. Mississippi, unlike many states, accepts mail-in ballots that arrive five days after Election Day, drawing out the counting process.

Ultimately, however, there is no legal path to a recount in the state. Derek Muller, a professor and expert on election law at the University of Notre Dame, said that a losing candidate could instead pursue a legal challenge over the inclusion of specific ballots or sets of ballots, which could result in a change in vote totals.

Fountain for The New York TimesAn unusual situation could be brewing in Mississippi, the only state in the country with no legal provision that allows for a recount of votes in a statewide election.The Democratic candidate for Senate, Scott Colom, had a narrow 65-vote lead over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, in the afternoon. His lead grew to 1,138 by the evening, but Mississippi’s secretary of state reported that about 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots could still arrive within the allotted five business days, and that there were also an “unknown number of affidavit ballots.”Some 47 states have a provision for an automatic recount if a contest is close or if a candidate requests a recount. Two more states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.Most state recount provisions were instituted during the last century as a result of legal challenges that made their way to state supreme courts. But Mississippi has no recount law on the books, leaving it unprepared to handle a particularly close election.There are still small batches of ballots to be counted in the state, and the margin between the candidates may widen. Mississippi, unlike many states, accepts mail-in ballots that arrive five days after Election Day, drawing out the counting process.Ultimately, however, there is no legal path to a recount in the state. Derek Muller, a professor and expert on election law at the University of Notre Dame, said that a losing candidate could instead pursue a legal challenge over the inclusion of specific ballots or sets of ballots, which could result in a change in vote totals.

A new political era opened in Washington on Wednesday, as Democrats vowed to use their sweeping majority to check President Trump’s power, while prominent Republicans blamed their midterm wipeout on his agenda and party leadership.

Democrats were on track to secure at least a 50-seat majority in the House and solid control of the Senate after notching seismic victories around the country, in deep red House districts and long-Republican Senate seats. Vice President JD Vance blamed the rout on Mr. Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran, a remarkable break from a president who, for much of the past decade, has demanded total fealty from his party.

“Everyone knows why we lost,” Mr. Vance said on social media. For his part, Mr. Trump said Mr. Vance’s assessment was “largely true.” He added, “If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House, predicted Democrats would win at least 255 of the 435 seats in the chamber, comparing the scope of his party’s romp to an “American tsunami.” Democrats picked off Republicans who had not expected competitive races in conservative-leaning seats from Indiana to Missouri to Alabama, putting themselves on pace to make generational gains similar to those of the Republican wave of 1994 — only in reverse.

After two years of Republican control of Congress that reduced the House’s role to that of mere bystander, Mr. Jeffries promised to reassert the chamber’s power by undertaking aggressive investigations with oversight.

“The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” Mr. Jeffries promised.

Republicans lost Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Two other tight Senate contests haven’t been called: Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi, where roughly 1,100 votes separated the two candidates as of Wednesday evening.

The decisive control of the Senate is a “generational remake,” Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, told reporters in Washington.

Voters across every major demographic group — race, age, gender and education — made a drastic swing left in Tuesday’s election, reversing the gains Mr. Trump had made with them in 2024.

Mr. Trump seemed to brush off the sweeping repudiation. He used his first public appearance on Wednesday to tour the site of the ballroom he is building on the White House grounds. There, he defended what he considered to be his legacy-defining projects. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world,” he said.

The shock waves from the election reverberated more resoundingly among other Republicans, who had feared widespread losses but had not anticipated such a renunciation of their party.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana told aides that he would not seek to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, setting off a scramble among ambitious Republicans to succeed him. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio announced he would seek the role, arguing that Republicans needed to take a combative approach toward the Democratic majority next year.

“In these next two years, our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democrat party is,” he said. “Offense, not defense, wins elections.”

Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana also jumped into the contest, arguing that Republicans must act with more unity.

These Republicans bet big on Trump. It didn’t pay off.

President Trump used to gloat about his near-perfect endorsement record, reveling in the control he exerted over the Republican nomination process during this year’s primary season. Voters overwhelmingly rewarded the candidates he backed and punished those who displeased him, muscling numerous less loyal candidates out of contention.

“If you pushed back” on Mr. Trump, said Justin Evans, a Republican strategist in South Carolina, “you’d get your head chopped off.”

Mr. Trump has little to brag about this week. Senate candidates he had helped elevate, including Darline Graham in South Carolina, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Ken Paxton in Texas, lost by margins previously unimagined by even the most optimistic Democrats. Those high-profile defeats contributed to what Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, a one-time Trump rival for the presidential nomination, called as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” as the country has seen in a century.

“The people who did the best last night were the people who distanced themselves from the president,” Mr. Evans said, calling the results “a universal repudiation of the bullying that’s been taking place during this primary” by Mr. Trump.

Here’s a look at what happened to some of the candidates who tied their fortunes most closely to Mr. Trump.

Darline Graham

After Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican, died in July, Mr. Trump threw his weight behind Mr. Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, in a snap primary election. While many Republican insiders objected, primary voters listened, narrowly nominating Ms. Graham over Representative Ralph Norman, despite her self-described lack of experience or policy expertise.

On Tuesday, the wider South Carolina electorate rejected Ms. Graham, choosing to send a Democrat to Washington for the first time in nearly 30 years.

“It wasn’t that voters rebuked Trump,” Mr. Evans said, noting that the Republican nominee for governor had earned at least 90,000 more votes than Ms. Graham. “It was that the entire Washington machine pushed this woman on South Carolina, and South Carolina resoundingly pushed back.”

Ken Paxton

Senate Republicans begged Mr. Trump to endorse Senator John Cornyn over Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, in the state’s Republican Senate primary. Many argued that Mr. Paxton’s scandal-ridden past would make it significantly more difficult, and more costly, to win in a general election. They also said a contentious intraparty battle would waste resources needed in more competitive states. Mr. Trump ignored them, waiting until days before a May primary runoff to back Mr. Paxton.

On Tuesday, despite dramatically outspending Democrats, Republicans lost the Senate seat, the governor’s mansion, and every other statewide race in Texas, breaking a more than three-decade-long streak of G.O.P. dominance.

Some Texas Republicans speculated that Mr. Paxton would have won the primary regardless of Mr. Trump’s choice. It is also not clear that Mr. Cornyn could have defied the tsunami of voter anger that propelled Democrats to victory up and down the ballot. But some blamed Mr. Paxton, and Mr. Trump, for the extent of the losses.

“You stand by Trump at your own peril at this point,” said Dade Phelan, the former Republican speaker of the State House. He recalled how Mr. Trump asked voters in Texas and elsewhere to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

“Well, voters imagined he was on the ballot,” Mr. Phelan said. “And it was an absolute apocalypse for Republicans.”

Michael Whatley

Mr. Trump’s fingerprints were all over North Carolina’s Senate race. First, Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who has served in North Carolina for more than a decade, announced he would retire rather than run for re-election after the president threatened to back a primary opponent against him.

Then, Mr. Trump handpicked Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, and Mr. Whatley spent millions touting Mr. Trump’s endorsement ahead of his victory in the Republican Senate primary. On Tuesday night, Mr. Whatley fell to former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, by around 20 points, a stunning leftward shift for a state that Mr. Trump won in 2024.

Meghan McMichael, 33, a voter in Canton, N.C., said on Tuesday that she had voted for Mr. Cooper and other Democrats in order to hold the Trump administration accountable for its treatment of immigrants, and the state of the economy.

“I’m just hopeful that certain people will be held accountable for things that have happened over the last two years,” she said.

Jon Husted

Senator Jon Husted, Ohio’s Republican Senate nominee and a former professional football player, was little known nationally until President Trump started talking about his rear end while on the campaign trail. Mr. Husted also joined Mr. Trump at several Ohio rallies in the final weeks of the campaign, tying himself to the president.

Mr. Husted lost to former Senator Sherrod Brown on Tuesday, making Ohio one of seven states that Democrats had flipped as of Wednesday evening.

The president’s comments about Mr. Husted’s backside may also have backfired, with voters across the country telling The New York Times they had disapproved of his remarks that Mr. Husted had a “great ass” and a “pile of muscle.”

In Lincoln, Neb., on Tuesday, Deondre Webster, 36, said he didn’t believe Mr. Trump is a good role model for his three daughters.

“We don’t want to see the leader of the country talking about male behinds or stuff like that onstage,” he said. “When he’s supposed to be the leader, and that’s not what we’re teaching our kids.”

Mark Barrett in North Carolina and Justin Diep in Nebraska contributed reporting.

What we know, and don’t, in the Alaska and Mississippi Senate vote counts.

Control of the U.S. Senate has already been determined, with 33 of the 35 contests being called within hours of polls closing. In Alaska and Mississippi, however, no race calls have been made for the Senate and it could be quite some time until either contest is decided, even as some additional vote totals trickle out in the coming days.

In both cases, the Democratic nominee is clinging to a slim lead, but the reasons for the lack of a call are far different.

What We Know in the Alaska Senate Race

Alaska’s Senate race could take days or weeks to be called. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, had a lead of fewer than 1,000 votes as of Wednesday afternoon, but nearly a quarter of the expected votes remain uncounted.

The bulk of the remaining vote is in the form of mail-in ballots. Some were cast close to Election Day, while others were postmarked by Election Day and will be received in the days after. A smaller chunk of early in-person ballots are also outstanding.

The deadline to tabulate all ballots, including provisional ballots, is Nov. 18. That is also the date that ranked-choice tabulation will begin, should neither Ms. Peltola nor Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, cross the 50 percent threshold needed to win the election in the first round.

While the late mail vote typically leans toward Democrats, multiple factors could undercut Ms. Peltola’s possible advantage, including how many ballots will be received and how many are from voters who did not rank additional candidates beyond their first choice. There is also the potentially confounding presence of the other two candidates on the ballot, Gerald L. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

A New York Times analysis of the available ranked-choice data pulled from each voter’s ballot shows that more than a third of voters who ranked Mr. Heikes or Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. as their first choice did not rank another candidate. That means these ballots would not count toward either Ms. Peltola or Senator Sullivan in subsequent rounds of the ranked-choice tabulation.

What We Know in the Mississippi Senate Race

As of Wednesday evening, Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee in Mississippi, had a lead of roughly 1,000 votes over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent. Because the margin is so tight, The Associated Press may not be able to make a race call until the state certifies a winner.

Mississippi is somewhat of an outlier in that it does not have a mechanism for automatic recounts, and has no method for a candidate to contest the election, so a court order would be required to initiate a recount.

Nearly all of the votes have been counted in the race, but a smattering of provisional ballots — which are ballots given to those with questions about their eligibility to vote — are still waiting to be counted, as are some late-arriving mail ballots. According to Mississippi's secretary of state, there are approximately 3,600 outstanding mail ballots that could arrive in time to be counted.

Mississippi’s Supreme Court ruled in June that the state must accept mail-in ballots that arrive by the Tuesday after Election Day — this year, Nov. 10. And provisional ballots in the state must be tallied by that day as well. For a provisional ballot to be accepted, the voter is required to provide proper identification to elections officials, obtain a state voter ID card, or submit a religious exemption.

Some counties in the state have said they hope to begin releasing some results of provisional ballots on Wednesday. It is currently unknown how many ballots remain uncounted statewide. Adding a layer of complexity, ballot processing and counting, which includes ruling on provisional ballots, is conducted by each county’s five-person elections commission rather than a single elections official.

In 2024, the state had just under 15,000 provisional ballots, of which 70 percent were accepted. In 2022, the state had about 5,700 provisional ballots, of which 75 percent were accepted.

A group that champions electing conservative women to public office issued a blunt warning to Republicans on Wednesday after the Democratic sweep of Congress, calling the defeats of a large number of G.O.P. women an emergency that must be addressed.

“We are once again facing a crisis-level decline in Republican women in Congress,” Danielle Barrow, the president of Winning For Women Action Fund, an outside group dedicated to electing Republican women, said in a statement.

Ms. Barrow sounded the alarm as Democrats were celebrating their own milestone of electing more than 100 women to the House for the first time in history.

Republicans already have far less gender diversity in their ranks in the House, where there are currently 32 G.O.P. women (including two nonvoting delegates) — around 15 percent of their members.

With the landslide Democratic victories that are projected to win them the largest House majority in decades, that number could potentially dip to below 20 next year, after all races are called.

In 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected just one new G.O.P. woman to Congress, the party made a commitment to recruit and invest in female candidates, Ms. Barrow said. It worked: Two years later, 11 of the 15 seats Republicans flipped were by women.

“But that commitment to recruiting women faded when the urgency did,” she said. “Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve. It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

Democrats eye inquiries into Trump actions on energy, public land.

Democrats in Congress are poised to ramp up investigations into Trump administration efforts to limit renewable energy development, promote fossil fuels and mining, and open up public lands to commercial interests.

Before the elections, House Democrats had already announced probes into some of those actions, including a $1 billion payout to cancel offshore wind farms, cuts to renewable energy investments in Puerto Rico and the shrinking of two national monuments in Utah. In other cases, they have raised allegations of corruption against officials overseeing public lands, fisheries and offshore energy development.

But with a majority in Congress next year, they can deepen those inquiries, said Representative Jared Huffman, Democrat of California, who stands to be chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee as its current ranking member. In January, Democrats will gain power to convene hearings, call witnesses to testify under oath and go to court to compel cooperation by the executive branch. Under Republican control, Congress has not used those powers to look into the Trump administration.

Just in the hours since the scope of the Democratic gains became clear, outside groups also began clamoring for new inquiries into steps by the administration to limit enforcement of pollution regulations and reduce the flow of federal disaster aid.

Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, said such investigations could help deliver on his party’s campaign promises to promote affordability. The Trump administration’s efforts to purge the government of any focus on climate change have contributed to rising property insurance premiums and energy costs, Mr. Whitehouse said.

“Democrats will work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors through their climate denial fraud and corrupting dark money influence,” Mr. Whitehouse said in a statement.

The Environmental Protection Network, a nonpartisan group of hundreds of former Environmental Protection Agency officials, called for investigations into Trump administration pollution-limit rollbacks and rule exemptions. The group said the administration has ignored scientific evidence and its own experts to put industry above public health.

Samantha Montano, a professor of emergency management at the Massachusetts Maritime Academy who has criticized the Trump administration’s disaster management policy, said Democrats should investigate staffing cuts at the Federal Emergency Management Agency, as well as the agency’s distribution of key preparedness grants and recovery funding. Analyses have shown a partisan bias in President Trump’s approval of federal disaster declarations, which unlock FEMA aid for communities.

‘I was caught up in the Trump tsunami’: Susan Collins speaks about losing her Senate seat.

As Susan Collins campaigned in York County, Maine, recently, a woman approached to inform the Republican senator that she had always supported her and “absolutely” loved her. But she wasn’t going to vote for her this time.

“She said it was the only way she could send a message to Trump,” Ms. Collins recounted in an interview on Wednesday, a day after she lost to the Democrat Troy Jackson in her attempt to win a sixth term.

That was the story of the election for Ms. Collins, the chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee and a force in the Senate for three decades.

“I was caught up in the Trump tsunami that swept away many incumbent Republican senators who have served their states well for many years and really care about our country,” she said.

The five-term Republican senator had long seemed invulnerable to the ordinary laws of politics because of her singular political brand as a New England centrist with a gift for constituent service and an ability to steer federal dollars back home. In 2008, she triumphed in Maine while Barack Obama was romping and other Republicans were falling. In 2020, it seemed like her number might be up when polls had her down against a well-funded state lawmaker, but she again won easily.

Democrats saluted ruefully in respect.

But 2026 turned out to be a different case entirely as Ms. Collins was brought down by a combination of factors, most of which were attributable to President Trump and the war with Iran. There were soaring fuel prices in a state reliant on home heating oil. The punishing tariffs the president imposed on neighboring Canada. An immigration crackdown that resulted in a fatal shooting by federal agents in one Maine community. And always the perception that she wasn’t doing enough to stand up to the president, even when she was one of the few Republicans to occasionally break with him.

“Everybody ignores the fact that I voted to convict him in the second impeachment trial,” Ms. Collins said. “What bigger break could there be? It is never enough. I want results and they want angry rhetoric.”

On top of dissatisfaction that she hadn’t distanced herself sufficiently from the president, some voters harbored resentment about her vote in 2018 to confirm Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, given his later role in overturning Roe v. Wade.

The coming result was evident from talking to voters on Tuesday as they exited the central polling place in Bangor — home turf for Ms. Collins. Several of them said they had repeatedly marked their ballots for “our senator,” as her ubiquitous yard signs proclaimed, but they would not do so this time.

“This time,” said Deborah Hanson of Bangor, “I’ve got to try something new. Susan Collins has voted with Trump on so many things.”

“To me, it is a close thing,” said Bob Kelly, another longtime Bangor voter. “But I can’t support anybody that supports Trump.”

In rejecting Ms. Collins, Maine voters gave up a tremendous amount of influence over federal spending by turning out the woman at the helm of the influential committee that controls federal spending. It is unusual but not unheard-of for voters to reject senior leaders.

Voters in Washington State dumped Representative Tom Foley, a Democrat, when he was speaker of the House in 1994. Senator Tom Daschle, the Democratic leader, lost his re-election bid to Senator John Thune, now the majority leader, in South Dakota in 2004.

Ms. Collins leaned heavily on her role in spending as she campaigned around the state, visiting the fire stations, community projects and infrastructure improvements for which she had secured funding, noting that if she were no longer in office, that money might dry up.

“I wanted to make sure people know what their choice was,” she said.

The man who defeated her, Mr. Jackson, will be a junior member of the Senate with little ability to steer to the state anywhere near the kind of financial aid that Ms. Collins had helped win.

“What she has been able to do over the last six years is extraordinary,” said Steve Abbott, her campaign manager and longtime senior aide. “Every town you go to, you see a project that was funded and work that needed to be done. That’s an opportunity that the state has walked away from.”

Up until the end, Ms. Collins and her team had hoped they could pull out a win as they watched from a hotel suite in Bangor. They had been cheered by the “rock star” reception they received around the state, an outpouring they said was better than during some of her winning races in the past.

“We went all over the state and I’ve got to tell you, the crowds were huge, the reception was warm and the response could not have been better,” Ms. Collins said as she addressed and thanked supporters in Bangor before the results were known.

But results from the Democratic stronghold of Portland overwhelmed her.

The race was chaotic, and Ms. Collins and her advisers like to note that they basically had to run against three opponents: Gov. Janet Mills, who initially appeared to be the likely challenger before she dropped out; the oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary but dropped out after sexual abuse allegations; and Mr. Jackson, who had lost the state’s Democratic primary for governor but was then selected to replace Mr. Platner on the ballot.

Democrats have been frustrated for years both by Ms. Collins herself and their inability to defeat her. They poured huge amounts of money into the campaign, trying to highlight her ties to Mr. Trump and her votes for his policies. Ms. Collins pushed back, noting her own differences with the president on the Iran war, tariffs, the immigration crackdown and safety net cuts.

Over the course of her career, Ms. Collins was at the center of many major legislative negotiations on such tough issues as gun safety, health care and, following the Jan. 6, 2021, assault at the Capitol, a bill overhauling how electoral votes were counted. Her absence in the Senate will be felt on big legislative fights. She has not missed a vote in her Senate tenure.

Her political career was inspired in part by Margaret Chase Smith, the Maine Republican who served in the Senate from 1949 to 1972. Ms. Collins once met Ms. Smith, who had delivered a famous denunciation of Joseph McCarthy, and noted that some constituents encouraged her to have a Smith-like moment of conscience when it came to Mr. Trump.

“I would argue that I have, like Margaret Chase Smith, taken a lot of tough votes and stood up for what I believe in,” she said. “But I think the best comparison is we each lost our last race for the Senate.

“I have now had my Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

Among the Democratic winners in Tuesday night’s elections: More medical professionals.

About a half-dozen Democrats who flipped Republican congressional seats are doctors and nurses, many of whom made health policy and their opposition to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s agenda central to their campaigns.

Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, a pediatrician, repeatedly called out Mr. Kennedy as her “archnemesis.” She and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan appear to be the first Democrats with medical degrees elected to the Senate in about 60 years.
